newsitem.title: MALAYSIA: FEATURE - Malaysia bets future on field of dreams.
newsitem.headline: FEATURE - Malaysia bets future on field of dreams.

text.p: It was a glimpse into the future.

Malaysian Prime Minister Mahathir Mohamad fed a "smart card" into a computer, which in a voice like Darth Vader, told a silver object resembling something from "Star Wars" to drill a hole atop a hill.
Thus was launched futuristic Cyberjaya, touted as the world's first planned multimedia city, on 7,000 hectares (17,300 acres) of Malaysia's past -- old rubber and oil palm estates.
Also known as "Cybercity", the groundbreaking on May 17 was the latest in a series of ambitious schemes aimed at making Malaysia an industrialised nation in the next quarter-century.

Cyberjaya is one of several major projects in the Multimedia Super Corridor (MSC), a 15- by 50-km (nine-by-30 miles) zone stretching south from Kuala Lumpur to where a new "paperless" federal capital and a "cyberspace" international airport are also under construction.
The MSC aims to draw world-class information technology companies -- build a corridor and they will come, to paraphrase a line from the Kevin Costner movie "Field of Dreams".
But sceptics wonder if mega-projects like the MSC are creating a firm foundation for future growth or, if like the groundbreaking ceremony, it is all a bit illusory.
"They are entering uncharted territory," said Bernard Tan, technology analyst with Merrill Lynch in Singapore. "It is going to be a difficult project."
So far, it is a huge property project.
Anchoring the northern point are the Petronas Towers. Rising 452 metres (1,482 feet), the glass-walled twin towers, vaguely resembling Islamic minarets, are the world's tallest.
Malaysia has also begun to build the world's longest building. Gigaworld, supported by stilts, will snake for 1.8 km (1.1 miles) over the Klang River in Kuala Lumpur.
For Malaysia's boosters, the projects symbolise the country's soaring ambitions and an attitude encapsulated in the national slogan, "Malaysia Boleh", or Malaysia can.
CRITICS FEAR OVER-DEPENDENCY ON CONSTRUCTION
But for the doubtful -- Mahathir calls them envious -- they are part of the prime minister's "edifice complex", an over-dependency on construction for economic growth.

Malaysia's economy has enjoyed a decade of stunning growth on the back of a massive inflow of mostly Japanese and American investment into the manufacturing sector, much of it located in sprawling industrial parks in the northern island of Penang.
The country is now one of the world's leading exporters of semiconductors, computer parts and appliances, mostly assembling goods from imported kits and components.
But with widespread labour shortages, Malaysia can no longer compete with its more populous and less developed neighbours for this kind of relatively low-tech assembly operations.
Penang, though, could be the model for the super corridor as Malaysia tries to clamber up the technology ladder and replace labour-intensive industries with capital-intensive ones.

As with Penang more than a decade ago, Malaysia is offering tax holidays and 100 percent equity stakes for foreign companies basing operations in the corridor. Parliament is expected to pass a series of "cyber laws" this year that would put Malaysia in the global forefront at removing barriers to multimedia communications.
The corridor will be served by a 2.5-10 gigabyte fibre optic backbone. The government is building a Multimedia University and other "intelligent townships" for future "knowledge workers".
Malaysia plans to soon introduce the world's first all-purpose "smart card". It would be used as a credit card, for identification and for access control, among other things.
MANPOWER, MANPOWER, MANPOWER
"All those things are not important," says Merrill Lynch's Tan. "What is important is manpower, manpower, manpower."
Malaysia promises easy work visas for foreign experts and fast-track procedures for imported equipment.

Despite shortages and escalating wages, the workforce is relatively well-educated and English is widely spoken. Its Chinese, Malay and Indian communities speak Asia's main languages for firms developing products for regional markets.

"But what is there that cannot be found elsewhere?", Tan said. "Anybody who takes a walk through Silicon Valley (California) will find dozens of languages and ethnic Asians. Why do they want to go halfway around the world to find it?
"It's not obvious what the advantages are."
Analysts say the best thing the corridor has going for it is Mahathir, who has proven sceptics wrong with his other projects, like the now successful Proton car.
"We are going to be very business-friendly," Mahathir told Reuters in an interview. "We have a greenfield site where people can develop whatever they want without any hindrance."

This unfettered oasis would be in contrast to the rest of the country, where work visas require up to nine months to process and a simple imported video-conferencing system takes at least four months to clear customs and licensing procedures.
Censorship is an issue in a country where the local media is licensed, foreign magazines take days to pass the censor and films that show kissing or too much skin are crudely edited.
ALARM BELLS RINGING FOR PROPERTY MARKET
The corridor is being built at a time when alarm bells are going off about the property market.

Cyberjaya -- which eventually will support a population of 240,000 with every home hooked up to the Internet and all transactions done by smart cards -- and the new capital of Putrajaya will have their first occupants a year from now.
The government's move out of Kuala Lumpur will leave a bunch of empty offices in its already glutted property market.

Greater Kuala Lumpur will have 2.03 million square metres of new office space by 1999, nearly doubling the total to about 5.6 million. The 88-story twin towers will put 371,000 square metres on the market.
Annual demand is seen at only around 278,000 square metres.
The central bank, expressing fears the glut could create a speculative bubble in the economy, imposed "preemptive" curbs on bank loans for property and share market purchases on April 1.

The move, following a banking crisis in neighbouring Thailand over the property market there, frightened investors who have deserted Malaysia's stock market in droves. The main board on the Kuala Lumpur Stock Exchange lost 114 billion ringgit ($45 billion) in market capitalisation from March 28 to May 16.
Analysts say companies are heavily leveraged in property, with corporate earnings channelled into land and building assets. Bank loans are routinely collateralised by property.
Few, however, expect a Thai-style crash.

"While we do not believe the Malaysian property market is heading towards a crash," SBC Warburg said in a recent report on the Malaysian economy, "the overbuilding of commercial and retail properties in Kuala Lumpur could potentially trigger a market collapse if left unchecked."
MALAYSIA'S ECONOMIC FUNDAMENTALS SOUND

Malaysia's economic fundamentals remain sound. The inflation rate was 2.6 percent year-on-year in April, the lowest in years. The country is entering its 10th year of over eight percent annual growth and the trade balance shows a robust surplus.
Base lending rates are relatively high at around nine percent and the ringgit has strengthened against most major currencies this year, drawing a steady influx of foreign funds.
The Geneva-based World Economic Forum recently ranked Malaysia as the world's ninth most competitive economy.
A total of 158 billion ringgit in infrastructure projects is under construction or will be built over the next three years.

Some of it is in the super corridor, but mostly it is for roads, ports, airports and power projects, all aimed at making Malaysia even more globally competitive. That should cushion any downturn in the property market, analysts said. ($1 = 2.50 ringgit)
